title: SQL Day 6 — NULLs, Data Quality & Conditional Logic
description: Handle missing values safely and validate data quality before using fields in business reporting.

teaching.teacher: ## NULL\nNULL represents missing or unknown data. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; equality operators do not correctly test NULL.
teaching.explain: A NULL is not the same as zero, empty text, or false.
teaching.detailedlearning: Always decide whether missing data should be excluded, flagged, or replaced before calculating KPIs.
teaching.expose: Missing values can silently change counts and averages.
teaching.example: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE postal_code IS NULL;
teaching.business_question: Data quality wants the number of orders without postal codes.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS missing_postal_codes FROM orders WHERE postal_code IS NULL;

questions.scenario: The team suspects missing customer identifiers.
questions.request: Return the number of rows where customer_id is NULL.

questions.scenario: Shipping records may have missing ship dates.
questions.request: Return order ID and customer name for rows with a missing ship date.

questions.scenario: Finance wants to know whether any profit values are missing.

questions.validation: NULL count divided by total rows

topics.title: COALESCE — Safe Defaults
topics.business_skill: Replace NULL with an explicit fallback when business logic requires it.

teaching.teacher: ## COALESCE\nCOALESCE returns the first non-NULL expression.
teaching.explain: It is useful when a report requires a display or calculation default.
teaching.detailedlearning: Do not blindly convert NULL to zero; only do so when zero is a valid business interpretation.
teaching.expose: A default value is a business decision, not merely a SQL convenience.
teaching.example: SELECT COALESCE(postal_code, 0) AS postal_code FROM orders;
teaching.business_question: The reporting team wants missing discount values treated as zero for a calculation.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT AVG(COALESCE(discount,0)) AS avg_discount FROM orders;

topics.title: NULL-Safe Conditional Logic
topics.business_skill: Combine CASE and NULL handling without misclassifying missing data.

teaching.teacher: ## NULL-aware CASE\nCASE can explicitly detect missing values before other business rules.
teaching.explain: Place the NULL rule where it matches the intended classification priority.
teaching.detailedlearning: Separate Unknown from real zero or negative values when data quality matters.
teaching.expose: Do not let ELSE accidentally hide missing-data problems.
teaching.example: CASE WHEN profit IS NULL THEN 'Missing' WHEN profit < 0 THEN 'Loss' ELSE 'Profit' END
teaching.business_question: Finance wants missing profit clearly separated from losses.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, CASE WHEN profit IS NULL THEN 'Missing' WHEN profit < 0 THEN 'Loss' ELSE 'Profit' END AS profit_status FROM orders;

questions.scenario: Finance needs missing profit distinguished from loss.
questions.request: Create Missing, Loss, and Profit labels.

topics.title: NULL Impact on Aggregates
topics.business_skill: Understand how missing values affect COUNT and AVG.

teaching.teacher: ## Aggregate behavior\nCOUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) ignores NULLs; AVG(column) also ignores NULL values.
teaching.explain: Two counts can legitimately differ when the column contains missing values.
teaching.detailedlearning: When reporting completeness, compare total rows with populated-field counts.
teaching.expose: An average over populated values is not necessarily an average over all records.
teaching.example: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, COUNT(discount) AS discount_rows, AVG(discount) AS avg_discount FROM orders;
teaching.business_question: The manager wants discount completeness and average discount.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, COUNT(discount) AS discount_rows, AVG(discount) AS avg_discount FROM orders;

teaching.teacher: ## Data-quality snapshot\nCombine counts and percentages to expose missingness before business KPIs are trusted.
teaching.explain: A quality query should make the size of the issue measurable.
teaching.detailedlearning: Choose critical columns based on business impact rather than checking every field indiscriminately.
teaching.expose: Data quality is part of analysis, not an afterthought.
teaching.example: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, SUM(CASE WHEN customer_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS missing_customer_ids FROM orders;
teaching.business_question: The analytics lead wants a quality snapshot for customer ID, region, and profit.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, SUM(CASE WHEN customer_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS missing_customer_ids, SUM(CASE WHEN region IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS missing_regions, SUM(CASE WHEN profit IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS missing_profit FROM orders;
